body.objective: Students will be able to use blocking and stage directions.

body.hook: Blocking is the choreography of a play: where each actor stands, when they cross, when they sit. Directors write it in a kind of shorthand so everyone can repeat the same moves every night.

vocabulary.definition: The planned movements and positions of actors on stage.

study.title: Plan the Moves
study.question: How does blocking help tell the story?
study.passage:
Blocking guide (written for this lesson):
Shorthand: X = cross; DSR, DSC, DSL, SR, CS, SL, USR, USC, USL = stage areas; ent = enter; ex = exit; sit, stand, kneel; → = toward. Example: "MAYA ent SR, X DSC" means Maya enters stage right and crosses downstage centre.
Blocking rules: 1. Move for a reason (a character crosses because they want something). 2. Keep an open position. 3. Avoid standing directly in front of another actor. 4. Cross in front of others on the downstage side when possible. 5. Use stage areas for meaning: the powerful character can take centre; someone avoiding conversation can move far upstage.
Task: Block your Maya and Jordan scene. Jordan starts sitting USL with a book. Write blocking for each beat in the margin of your script. Then run it twice so the moves become automatic.

body.objective: Students will be able to plan props and costumes.
body.iCan: I can plan props and costumes.
successCriteria: I can choose props and costume pieces that support character and story
I can create a props and costume list
I can handle props safely and consistently
body.hook: A single prop can tell the audience everything: a crown says royalty, a stethoscope says doctor, a crumpled letter says bad news. Simple costumes and props, chosen carefully, make a scene believable without a big budget.

vocabulary.definition: An object an actor uses on stage.
A small prop carried by an actor, such as a phone or a book.
A larger item on the set, such as a chair or table.
A single item of clothing that suggests a character, such as a hat or scarf.
A table offstage where props are set out in order.
Placing props and set pieces before the scene begins.

study.title: Small Things, Big Meaning
study.question: How do props and costumes support a scene?
study.passage:
Design task (written for this lesson):
1. Analyze (10 minutes): Read your Maya and Jordan scene for prop and costume clues. Stage directions say Jordan has a book; where are they? A library? A classroom at lunch? What would each character wear? What might Maya carry (a phone with a photo of the list)?
2. Choose (10 minutes): Select no more than three props and two costume pieces per character. Each must tell the audience something: a team jacket Jordan never zips up; a worn library book; Maya's phone.
3. Lists (10 minutes): Make a props list (item, character, when used, preset or carried, source) and a costume list (character, item, why).
4. Props table (10 minutes): Set up a props table with labelled spaces. Practise collecting and returning props.
5. Run (10 minutes): Run the scene with props and costumes. Note any problems: noise, dropped items, things that pull focus.

body.objective: Students will be able to rehearse with a stage manager.
body.iCan: I can rehearse with a stage manager.
successCriteria: I can describe the role of the stage manager
I can run a rehearsal with a stage manager and prompt book
I can take part in a dress rehearsal and polish a scene
body.hook: When the curtain rises, the most important person in the building might be someone the audience never sees: the stage manager. They call every cue, track every prop and keep rehearsals on schedule.

vocabulary.definition: The person who organizes rehearsals and runs the show backstage.
The stage manager's master script with blocking, cues and notes.
The stage manager's instruction to start a cue, such as "Lights, go."
A final rehearsal with costumes, props and all technical elements.
The call for actors to go to their starting positions.
When an actor asks the prompter for a forgotten line by saying "Line."

study.title: Running the Show
study.question: How does a stage manager help a scene come together?
study.passage:
Stage manager duties (written for this lesson): Before rehearsal: set up the space, preset props, check costumes. During rehearsal: follow the script, prompt lines, record blocking changes in the prompt book, time the scene. Before performance: call "Places, please," check everyone is ready. During performance: call cues ("Lights up, go"; "Music, go"), watch for problems. After: return props, write a rehearsal report.
Task: In groups of three, one person is the stage manager and two are actors.
1. SM sets up a prompt book: a copy of the script with blocking, props and two cues marked (lights up at the start, lights down at the end).
2. Rehearsal (15 minutes): SM runs the scene, prompts any "Line" call, notes changes.
3. Dress rehearsal (10 minutes): Full run with costumes, props and cues. SM calls places and cues.
4. Performance (10 minutes): Perform for the class.
5. SM writes a short rehearsal report: time, problems, notes for next time.
